rows.item: Basis to assume for C&W DFW $24.78 (inference)
rows.value: NNN (by C&W shopping-center convention; ±15% series uncertainty)
rows.source_title: Inference from C&W Q4 2015 national snapshot plus C&W Houston and San Diego Q2 2026 local reports
rows.quote: Rental rates reflect triple net asking $psf/annually for all tracked shopping center types. | Avg. Direct NNN Rent $21.52 (Houston Q2 2026) | *Rental rates reflect weighted triple net (NNN) asking $psf/month. (San Diego Q2 2026)
rows.notes: This is an inference. The current national report does not label the basis. Every C&W shopping-center source that does label it says NNN. The 2025 Weitzman Texas reports say asking rates exclude triple nets, and TAD finds 75% of in-place neighborhood-center leases are NNN. Model $24.78 as base rent with NNN on top.
rows.checker_evidence: All quoted pieces are accurate: TREC 2015 'Rental rates reflect triple net asking $psf/annually for all tracked shopping center types'; Houston 'Avg. Direct NNN Rent $21.52'; San Diego '*Rental rates reflect weighted triple net (NNN) asking $psf/month'. The Weitzman 2025 and 2026 reports say asking rates 'do not reflect concessions or triple nets' (San Antonio) and 'do not include NNN charges' (Austin). However, the Q2 2026 national table gives 'San Diego, CA ... $36.56' and 'Houston, TX ... $24.55'. Both are materially above the local NNN figures, and the gap is larger than ±15% for San Diego. The cause could be a different inventory or a different basis. The ±15% tolerance is not derived from any source, so the T2 label is overstated.
rows.corrected_value: NNN only as an unverified assumption (T3). C&W's national series runs well above C&W's own local NNN series for the same quarter: Houston $24.55 vs $21.52 NNN (+14%), and San Diego $36.56 vs $2.26x12 = $27.12 NNN (+35%). The stated ±15% band is therefore too narrow and has no source.
rows.value_final: NNN only as an unverified assumption (T3). C&W's national series runs well above C&W's own local NNN series for the same quarter: Houston $24.55 vs $21.52 NNN (+14%), and San Diego $36.56 vs $2.26x12 = $27.12 NNN (+35%). The stated ±15% band is therefore too narrow and has no source.

rows.item: Texas statutory deadline to refund a commercial security deposit
rows.unit: days after surrender and forwarding address
rows.source_title: Texas Property Code §93.005 (via Texas.Public.Law)
rows.quote: (a) The landlord shall refund the security deposit to the tenant not later than the 60th day after the date the tenant surrenders the premises and provides notice to the landlord or the landlord's agent of the tenant's forwarding address under Section 93.009
rows.notes: Statute text, added by Acts 2001. The Texas Legislature's own statute site is JavaScript-rendered and I could not read it, so I read the text on Texas.Public.Law. Useful for the deposit-refund mechanic at lease end.
rows.checker_evidence: Texas.Public.Law page, verbatim: '(a) The landlord shall refund the security deposit to the tenant not later than the 60th day after the date the tenant surrenders the premises and provides notice to the landlord or the landlord’s agent of the tenant’s forwarding address under Section 93.009 (Tenant’s Forwarding Address).' History: 'Added by Acts 2001, 77th Leg., ch. 1460, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 2001. Amended by Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 1143, Sec. 1'. The official statutes.capitol.texas.gov page is JavaScript-rendered and returned no text to curl. T1 is acceptable because the mirror reproduces the statute verbatim.

rows.item: Retail in-line store fit-out, U.S. national average (Cushman & Wakefield 2026)
rows.source_title: Cushman & Wakefield, 2026 U.S. Retail Fit Out Cost Guide (landing page)
rows.quote: National in-line retail fit out costs averaged $157 per square foot (psf) in 2026, up a modest 1.4% year-over-year (YOY) as softer demand offset ongoing labor and material pressures. Costs vary materially by market. Northern California ($217 psf), the Pacific Northwest ($202 psf), and New York City ($181 psf) are the most expensive markets, while the Midwest ($120 psf) and Southeast ($126 psf) remain the most cost-effective.
rows.notes: Based on a survey of 15 general contractors across 15 markets. This is a full contractor fit-out with branded finishes, so it runs higher than FDD second-gen figures. The Dallas/Texas figure is inside the flipbook, which could not be read.
rows.checker_evidence: C&W 2026 U.S. Retail Fit Out Cost Guide landing page (WebFetch): 'National in-line retail fit out costs averaged $157 per square foot (psf) in 2026, up a modest 1.4% year-over-year (YOY)... rows.item: Fort Worth retail tenant finish-out/remodel permits, declared job value per sq ft (2,500-15,000 sf, 2024-2026)

rows.quote: Computed: JobValue / SqFt for Permit_Type='Commercial Building Permit', Permit_SubType='Remodel', Specific_Use='Retail Store', File_Date >= 2024-01-01, SqFt 2,500-15,000, B1_WORK_DESC matching finish-out/tenant improvement/interior remodel/build-out, excluding roof, facade, sign, white-box/shell and suite-division jobs and Void/Withdrawn/Expired permits. n=28; p10 30.5, p25 52.3, median 92.4, p75 141.7, p90 247.2; median size 5,475 sf. Permits include PB24-16108, PB26-06077, PB26-06636, PB26-11093, PB26-06749, PB25-06988.
rows.notes: DFW-specific. The value is the contractor's declared construction value at permitting, which usually excludes loose fixtures and equipment. The sample leans toward national chains (Bath & Body Works, T-Mobile, Verizon, Dollar Tree, Pet Supplies Plus) and includes one $790/sf outlier, which the median absorbs.
rows.checker_evidence: I queried the CFW FeatureServer (Commercial Building Permit, Remodel, Retail Store, File_Date>=2024-01-01; 816 records across the 3 uses, deduplicated by Permit_No, Void/Withdrawn/Expired excluded, 2,500–15,000 sf), which leaves 61 retail-remodel permits. One variant (tenant improvement|build-out|remodel|renovat, excluding roof/facade/sign/white-box/warm-shell/retail-shell/suite-division) also gives p75 141.7, but p25 46.1 rather than 52.3. No variant reproduced all four quartiles and median size 5,475 at once. The figure is sensitive to the subjective description filter: reasonable variants give medians of roughly 69–126 $/sf. rows.item: Retail rate qualification test (primarily engaged in retail trade)
rows.value: >50% of revenue from retail/wholesale; <50% from own-produced products

rows.item: Franchise margin options 3/4: total revenue minus greater of $1M or (COGS or compensation, by election)

rows.item: Sales tax quarterly-filer threshold
rows.source_title: Texas Tax Code §151.401(b); 34 TAC §3.286(g)
rows.quote: (b) If a taxpayer owes less than $500 for a calendar month or $1,500 for a calendar quarter, the taxes are due and payable on the 20th day of the month following the end of the calendar quarter.

rows.item: Per-day (days-in-month-normalized) seasonality index, mean 2022–2025 — total retail, grocery 4451, clothing 448, electronics & appliance 443, pharmacies 44611
rows.unit: ratio of average daily sales in the month to the year's average daily sales
rows.source_title: Computed from Census mrtssales92-present.xlsx NOT ADJUSTED rows (same inputs as the monthly-index rows)
rows.quote: Formula: index_m = mean over 2022–2025 of (sales_m / days_in_month_m) / (annual TOTAL / days_in_year); days_in_year 365, 2024 = 366 (Feb 2024 = 29 days). Monthly inputs as quoted in the per-category monthly-index rows.
rows.notes: T1-derived. This is the multiplier to apply to a DAILY demand tick (it strips the 28/30/31-day effect, which is already produced by the calendar in a daily sim). Still contains trading-day mix (number of weekends) and within-year growth trend.

rows.item: Detrended (ratio to centered 2x12 moving average) seasonal factors, mean 2022–2025, renormalized to mean 1 — total retail, grocery 4451, clothing 448, electronics & appliance 443, pharmacies 44611
rows.unit: ratio of month sales to centered 12-month moving average (monthly, includes days-in-month effect)
rows.source_title: Computed from Census mrtssales92-present.xlsx NOT ADJUSTED rows, sheets 2021–2026
rows.quote: CMA_t = (0.5*S[t-6] + S[t-5..t+5] + 0.5*S[t+6]) / 12; factor_m = mean over Jan 2022–Dec 2025 of S_t/CMA_t, rescaled so the 12 factors average 1. Uses the 2021 sheet and Jan–Jun 2026 cells of the 2026 sheet (e.g. 44611 2026: 30922, 29408, 32717, 32140, 32194, 32725) in addition to the 2022–2025 inputs quoted above.
rows.notes: Classical multiplicative decomposition; removes the within-year growth bias. Differs from the simple index by <=0.013 except pharmacies (Jan +0.028, Dec -0.025) and total retail (Jan +0.012, Dec -0.012). Recommended source for pharmacy shape. Jul 2026 (preliminary) not used.
rows.checker_evidence: I recomputed the 2x12 centered moving average on the NSA series Jan 2021–Jun 2026, using the 2021 sheet plus the 2026 sheet. The 2026 44611 cells read 30922, 29408, 32717, 32140, 32194, 32725, matching the quote. I averaged the ratios over Jan 2022–Dec 2025 and rescaled to mean 1. All 60 values match the claim, e.g. TOTAL Jan 0.911, Dec 1.107; 4451 Jan 0.993, Dec 1.054; 448 Dec 1.550; 443 Dec 1.324; 44611 Jan 0.998, Oct 1.058, Dec 1.076. The VALUE is correct, but one statement in NOTES is slightly wrong. The notes say the difference from the simple index is '<=0.013 except pharmacies and total retail'. In fact grocery 4451 Jan differs by +0.0146 (0.993 vs 0.979) and clothing 448 Dec by -0.0144 (1.550 vs 1.564). Total retail's max is 0.012, so it is not an exception. Pharmacy (+0.027 Jan, -0.024 Dec) is right.

Weighted mean transactions per person-day: Mon 0.267, Tue 0.232, Wed 0.248, Thu 0.243, Fri 0.282, Sat 0.283, Sun 0.266; share = mean_d/sum. Bootstrap SE (1,000 respondent resamples) ±0.5-0.6 pts per day.
rows.notes: Per year: 2023 Mon 15.8/Tue 14.1/Wed 14.0/Thu 13.7/Fri 13.9/Sat 15.5/Sun 13.0; 2024 14.6/13.8/12.5/13.1/15.4/16.4/14.2; 2025 13.8/10.1/14.5/13.5/16.6/14.9/16.7. Implied count multipliers (share*7): Mon 1.03, Tue 0.89, Wed 0.95, Thu 0.94, Fri 1.09, Sat 1.09, Sun 1.02. Tuesday is the most consistent trough. Sanity check: the DCPC 2025 report says consumers made '37 purchases' per month (about 1.2/day), and this code gives about 1.16 non-bill payments per person-day in 2025.
rows.checker_evidence: Downloaded the DCPC 2023 and 2024 archive zips and the 2025 public CSV zip myself from atlantafed.org. Filters: day level diary_day 1-3 with non-missing daily_weight, giving 42,725 person-days and 15,167 respondent-years (matches). Day of week from assigned_day_week (codebook: 0=Sunday...6=Saturday). Transactions: payment==1, bill!=1, in_person==1, merch==1 (codebook: '1 - Grocery stores, convenience stores without gas stations, pharmacies'). Weighted mean counts are Mon 0.267, Tue 0.232, Wed 0.248, Thu 0.243, Fri 0.282, Sat 0.283, Sun 0.266, so shares are 14.7/12.7/13.6/13.4/15.5/15.5/14.6 with weekend 30.2 (exact match). Per-year shares match the notes exactly. Bootstrap (300 respondent resamples): per-day SE 0.52-0.68, weekend SE 0.87; the row says ±0.5-0.6 and ±0.8, slightly low. The DCPC 2025 report does say 'US consumers on average made 37 purchases and 10 bill payments per month'.
rows.corrected_value: Mon 14.7, Tue 12.7, Wed 13.6, Thu 13.4, Fri 15.5, Sat 15.5, Sun 14.6 (weekend 30.2 ± ~0.9). Per-day shares confirmed. rows.item: Fed Board card-transaction data (First Data): ranking of retail spending days
rows.value: Highest: Thursday, Friday, Saturday; lowest by far: Sunday; drifting toward Fri/Sat, away from Mon/Tue
rows.unit: qualitative ranking of daily transaction volume
rows.source_title: Aladangady, Aron-Dine, Dunn, Feiveson, Lengermann & Sahm, 'From Transactions Data to Economic Statistics', FEDS 2019-057, Federal Reserve Board
rows.quote: we find that retail transaction volumes vary markedly by the day of the week—the highest spending days appear to be Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, and the lowest spending day by far is Sunday. Interestingly, there also appears to be a slow shift in the composition of spending by day of week, toward Fridays and Saturdays and away from Mondays and Tuesdays.
rows.notes: No numeric shares were published. The 'retail' here is broad card spending (includes restaurants and services), which fits DCPC all-payments (Sunday lowest). Grocery-specific data show Sunday is not low.
rows.checker_evidence: Downloaded FEDS 2019-057 (pdftotext), Aladangady, Aron-Dine, Dunn, Feiveson, Lengermann and Sahm. Verbatim: 'we find that retail transaction volumes vary markedly by the day of the week—the highest spending days appear to be Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, and the lowest spending day by far is Sunday. Interestingly, there also appears to be a slow shift in the composition of spending by day of week, toward Fridays and Saturdays and away from Mondays and Tuesdays.' Minor note fix: the 'retail sales group' is 'total retail sales (including food services) excluding sales at building materials stores and gasoline stations'. It includes restaurants but not services in general.
rows.corrected_value: Highest: Thursday, Friday, Saturday; lowest by far: Sunday; drifting toward Fri/Sat, away from Mon/Tue
rows.value_final: Highest: Thursday, Friday, Saturday; lowest by far: Sunday; drifting toward Fri/Sat, away from Mon/Tue

The last row is "Plain whole milk: Per capita availability adjusted for loss,2021,Loss from retail/ institutional to consumer level-Percent,12,". The ERS LAFA documentation page (WebFetch, 'Last Updated 9/4/2026') says: "PG did not have appropriate data to update the retail-level loss assumptions for specific grains, dairy, and added fats & oils". This confirms the value is a fixed legacy assumption, not a yearly measurement.

rows.item: Bread DSD delivery frequency (Flowers/LePage distributors, Maine chain accounts)

rows.quote: Plaintiffs make deliveries five days a week, and on the other two days of the week they perform “recalls” or “pull ups” (two alternative names for the same thing) to adjust the stock on the shelves in the major customers’ stores. ... Certain of Plaintiffs’ accounts, most notably Hannaford’s and Walmart, require shelf and display attention every day
rows.notes: Rated T2: a primary court record, but it describes one bakery network's large-chain accounts in Maine, not small DFW stores. So the bakery side bears stale risk, not the retailer.

rows.item: Bread: scan-based trading and stale/returned product disposal (Flowers Foods)
rows.value: 221 thrift stores; $62.2 million FY2025 sales of returned and surplus product
rows.source_title: Flowers Foods, Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2025 (filed 2026-02-25)
rows.quote: We also sell returned and surplus product through a system of thrift stores. The company currently operates 221 such stores and reported sales of $62.2 million during Fiscal 2025 from these outlets. ... SBT technology allows the retailer to take ownership of our products when the consumer purchases the products rather than at the time they are delivered to the retailer.
rows.notes: Do not read this as a stale rate: thrift sales are at markdown prices and include surplus, against total sales of $5.3B. The design point is that under scan-based trading (SBT) bread is effectively consignment, so the store carries no stale-bread inventory risk.
rows.checker_evidence: Flowers 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 3, 2026 (SEC, curl; signatures dated February 25, 2026): "We also sell returned and surplus product through a system of thrift stores. The company currently operates 221 such stores and reported sales of $62.2 million during Fiscal 2025 from these outlets." Also: "SBT technology allows the retailer to take ownership of our products when the consumer purchases the products rather than at the time they are delivered to the retailer." Total sales: "Fiscal 2025 sales of $5.3 billion" ($5,256.5 million).
rows.corrected_value: 221 thrift stores; $62.2 million FY2025 sales of returned and surplus product
rows.value_final: 221 thrift stores; $62.2 million FY2025 sales of returned and surplus product

rows.item: Physical inventory count cadence (shrink true-up) at a Texas c-store chain
rows.source_title: Yesway, Inc., Form DRS/A (draft IPO registration statement)
rows.quote: Because the approximation of market under the retail inventory method is based on estimates such as markups, markdowns, and inventory losses (shrink), there exists an inherent uncertainty in the final determination of inventory cost and gross margin. In order to mitigate that uncertainty, the Company performs quarterly physical counts at all locations
rows.notes: Yesway is a convenience-store operator (Fort Worth-area HQ; not confirmed from this filing). The filing confirms that shrink is estimated between counts and trued up at quarterly physical counts. That maps cleanly to the game's monthly close plus a periodic count adjustment.
rows.checker_evidence: Yesway DRS/A (SEC, curl; "Confidential submission #2 ... December 22, 2025", Form S-1): "Because the approximation of market under the retail inventory method is based on estimates such as markups, markdowns, and inventory losses (shrink), there exists an inherent uncertainty ... the Company performs quarterly physical counts at all locations". rows.item: Implied monthly/daily geometric retention from Leone's 6-9 month duration (90% interval)
rows.source_title: Computation from Leone (1995)
rows.notes: Under the alternative convention λ^(n+1) = 0.1, monthly retention is 0.72-0.79. This is an upper bound on retention, because the 2017 meta-analysis gives a shorter interval for mass media.
rows.checker_evidence: Recomputed in python: 0.1^(1/6)=0.6813, 0.1^(1/9)=0.7743; daily 0.6813^(1/30.44)=0.9875 and 0.7743^(1/30.44)=0.9916; alternative 0.1^(1/7)=0.7197, 0.1^(1/10)=0.7943. The arithmetic is correct. Caveat: it rests on the unverified assumption that Leone's interval is a 90% duration interval. Clarke-style 90% duration intervals for a Koyck lag are often defined so that λ^(n+1)=0.1 (the row's 'alternative'), which may be the more standard convention (not verified against the paywalled original).

rows.item: Carryover meta-analysis (918 estimates): long-term share of total effect by communication type

rows.quote: The authors find the mean long-term shares of the total effect for personal selling (.687) and targeted advertising (.650) are distinctly larger than that for mass media advertising (.523)
rows.notes: In a Koyck model the long-term share equals the carryover coefficient λ, so total/short-term = 1/(1–.523) = 2.10 for mass media and 2.86 for targeted. This matches the Sethuraman LT/ST ratio of 2.0.
